title: Char Siu (Cantonese BBQ Pork)
description: Pork shoulder strips marinated overnight in hoisin, five-spice and honey, then roasted hot and basted until the edges char and caramelize — the pork behind every Cantonese roast-meat window.

ingredients.item: boneless pork shoulder, cut into 3cm-thick strips

ingredients.note: for basting, mixed with 1 tbsp hot water

steps: Combine hoisin sauce, light and dark soy sauce, sugar, Shaoxing wine, five-spice, salt, garlic and sesame oil in a bowl. Reserve 2 tablespoons of this marinade in the fridge for basting later.

Rub the rest of the marinade into the pork strips, cover, and refrigerate overnight (at least 8 hours) — this long marinate is what carries the flavor all the way through the meat, not just the surface.
Let the pork sit at room temperature for 20 minutes, then set a wire rack over a foil-lined tray with a little water in the tray to catch drips and prevent burning.
Roast at 220°C (425°F) for 20 minutes, then flip the strips and roast 10 more minutes.
Brush the strips with the reserved marinade, roast 5 minutes, flip and brush the other side, and roast a final 5 minutes until the edges are lightly charred.
Brush both sides with the honey-water glaze in the last 2 minutes for shine and a touch of char.
Rest 5 minutes, then slice against the grain and serve over rice or with steamed buns.
tips: Don't skip the overnight marinate — a few hours gives you seasoned pork, not char siu; the flavor needs time to penetrate the meat, not just coat it.
Watch the last 10 minutes closely: the sugar in the marinade caramelizes fast and goes from charred-good to burnt-bitter within a minute.
nutritionNote: Pork shoulder keeps enough fat to stay juicy through roasting and the marinade is sugar- and sodium-heavy, so serve slices over plain rice with a side of blanched greens rather than more roast meats at the same meal.

title: Cumin Beef Stir-Fry
description: Thin-sliced beef velveted and seared fast with whole toasted cumin seeds, dried chili and onion until smoky and fragrant — a home-cook take on the Xinjiang lamb skewer stall, built around beef instead.

ingredients.item: flank steak, thinly sliced against the grain
dried red chilies, snipped in half

steps: Massage the baking soda into the beef, then mix in the soy sauce, cornstarch and water. Marinate 15 minutes — the baking soda is what keeps thin-sliced flank tender in the short, hot cook.
Toast the cumin seeds in a dry pan over low heat for 1 minute until fragrant; set aside.
Heat a wok over high heat until smoking, add half the oil, and sear the beef in a single layer for 30-45 seconds per side until just browned; remove and set aside.
Add the remaining oil, then stir-fry the onion and bell pepper for about 1 minute until starting to soften but still crisp.
Add the garlic, dried chilies, chili flakes and toasted cumin seeds; stir-fry 20-30 seconds until fragrant.
Return the beef to the wok, sprinkle in the ground cumin, sugar and salt, and toss over high heat for 30-45 seconds until everything is well coated.
Scatter with cilantro and serve immediately over rice.
tips: Toasting the cumin seeds before they hit the hot oil doubles their aroma — don't skip straight to raw seeds in the wok.
Keep the sear on the beef fast and the wok hot throughout; cumin beef should taste smoky and charred at the edges, not steamed.
kidNote: The heat here comes from whole dried chilies and chili flakes rather than numbing Sichuan pepper, but it still runs hot. Cook the kids' portion separately: use half the chili flakes, skip the whole dried chilies entirely, and season with just the cumin, sugar and salt.
nutritionNote: A protein-forward, vegetable-light stir-fry, so round out the plate with a big side of blanched or stir-fried greens, and go easy on extra salt since the marinade and seasoning already carry sodium.

title: Soy Sauce Chicken
description: A whole chicken gently poached in a spiced soy sauce master stock until just cooked through, then bathed in the cooling liquid for silky, deeply seasoned meat and glossy amber skin — Cantonese roast-meat-shop cooking at home.

ingredients.note: for brushing the skin at the end

steps: Take the chicken out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking so it isn't cold going into the pot.

Heat the oil in a pot just large enough to hold the chicken. Add the ginger and scallion and cook over medium-low heat until fragrant and lightly caramelized, about 1 minute, then add the star anise and cinnamon.
Pour in the Shaoxing wine and let it bubble 1 minute, then add the light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, rock sugar and water. Bring to a simmer and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Lower the whole chicken breast-side down into the simmering sauce; it should be at least two-thirds submerged. Cover and simmer gently for 15 minutes.

Flip the chicken breast-side up, cover, and simmer another 15 minutes, then turn off the heat and let the chicken sit in the hot sauce, covered, for 20 minutes to finish cooking through without drying out.
Check doneness by piercing the thickest part of the thigh — the juices should run clear with no pink. Lift the chicken out and brush the skin with sesame oil for shine.
Rest 10 minutes, then chop into pieces and spoon some of the sauce over the top to serve.
Strain and save the remaining sauce; it keeps in the fridge for weeks and can be reused as a master stock for the next batch.
tips: Turning off the heat and letting the chicken finish in the residual heat of the sauce, rather than simmering it the whole time, is what keeps the breast meat silky instead of stringy.
Save the strained master sauce — each reuse gets more complex, and it's the traditional way this dish is made in Cantonese homes.
nutritionNote: The poaching method needs almost no added fat, but the sauce itself is concentrated soy and salty even diluted with water, so spoon it sparingly over the meat and serve with plain rice and a vegetable side rather than more sauce at the table.

title: Braised Beef Brisket with Daikon
description: Beef chuck and daikon radish simmered low and slow with star anise, ginger and a splash of soy until the meat is fall-apart tender and the radish has soaked up all the braising liquid — a Cantonese cold-weather stew built for rice.

ingredients.item: beef chuck or brisket, cut into 4cm chunks

ingredients.note: enough to cover the beef, plus more as it braises

ingredients.item: daikon radish, peeled and cut into thick chunks

steps: Cover the beef with cold water in a pot, bring to a boil, and blanch for 3 minutes to release scum; drain and rinse the beef and the pot.
Heat the oil in a clean pot over medium heat and fry the ginger, garlic and scallion until fragrant, about 1 minute.
Add the star anise, cinnamon and bay leaves, then the blanched beef; stir-fry 2 minutes until the beef picks up a little color.
Pour in the Shaoxing wine and let it bubble 1 minute, then add the light soy sauce, dark soy sauce, rock sugar and enough water to just cover the beef.
Bring to a boil, skim any remaining scum, then reduce to a low simmer, cover, and braise for 1.5 hours, topping up water if it runs low.
Add the daikon chunks and continue simmering, partially covered, for 45 minutes to 1 hour, until both the beef and daikon are fork-tender and the sauce has reduced and thickened slightly.
Taste and adjust salt if needed, discard the star anise, cinnamon and bay leaves if you can find them, and serve hot over rice, garnished with sliced scallion.
tips: Chuck holds up better than lean brisket over a long braise — brisket alone can turn dry and stringy by the time the daikon is done.
This tastes better the next day: refrigerate overnight so the flavor deepens, then reheat gently before serving.
nutritionNote: The daikon makes this a genuinely balanced one-pot meal with real vegetable content built in, and the fat renders out of the chuck as it braises, so serve with plain rice and skip adding extra oil-heavy sides at the same meal.

title: Garlic Eggplant
localTitle: Yu Xiang Qie Zi (鱼香茄子)
description: Chinese eggplant fried until silky-soft, then tossed with ground pork in the sweet-sour-spicy "fish fragrant" sauce of doubanjiang, garlic and vinegar — no fish involved, just Sichuan's most famous flavor blend built around a vegetable.

ingredients.item: Chinese or Japanese eggplant, cut into thick batons
doubanjiang (Pixian chili bean paste), finely chopped
scallion, whites and greens separated, chopped

steps: Cut the eggplant into thick batons, toss with the salt, and let sit 10 minutes to draw out moisture; pat dry with paper towels before cooking so it fries instead of steams.
Heat half the oil in a wok over medium-high heat and fry the eggplant in batches, turning occasionally, for 5-6 minutes per batch until soft and lightly browned all over; remove and set aside.
Add the remaining oil and brown the ground pork over medium-high heat, breaking it up, until it starts to crisp at the edges.
Push the pork to one side, add the doubanjiang to the cleared space, and stir-fry until the oil turns red, about 1 minute, then mix it through the pork.
Add the garlic, ginger and scallion whites; stir-fry 30 seconds until fragrant.
Return the eggplant to the wok along with the soy sauce, vinegar, sugar and stock. Simmer 2 minutes so the eggplant soaks up the sauce.
Stir in the cornstarch slurry and toss until the sauce thickens and coats everything glossy.
Scatter with scallion greens and serve hot over rice.
tips: Salting and drying the eggplant before frying keeps it from turning into an oil sponge — skip this step and the dish gets greasy fast.
The sauce should taste balanced between sweet, sour, salty and spicy at once; that combination, not any actual fish, is what "fish fragrant" refers to.
kidNote: Doubanjiang brings real heat here with no numbing peppercorn involved, but it's still too spicy as written for young kids. Set aside a plain portion of fried eggplant before the doubanjiang goes in, then finish the kids' share with just garlic, a spoon of soy sauce, a little vinegar and sugar.
nutritionNote: Frying the eggplant adds meaningful oil even after salting and draining, so blot the finished dish with a paper towel if serving small portions, and the doubanjiang and soy sauce both carry sodium, so skip extra salt elsewhere in the meal.

title: Stir-Fried Bok Choy with Mushrooms
description: Baby bok choy and shiitake mushrooms stir-fried hot and fast with garlic, then glazed with oyster sauce — the everyday vegetable side that shows up on nearly every Cantonese family dinner table.

ingredients.item: baby bok choy, halved or quartered lengthwise

steps: Wash the bok choy thoroughly, since dirt hides in the base, and halve or quarter each head lengthwise.
Stir together the oyster sauce, soy sauce, sugar and water or stock in a small bowl.
Heat the oil in a wok over high heat until shimmering, then add the garlic and stir-fry 10 seconds until fragrant.
Add the mushrooms and stir-fry 2 minutes until they soften and start to brown at the edges.
Add the bok choy and stir-fry 1-2 minutes until the leaves wilt and the stems turn bright green but stay crisp.
Pour in the sauce, toss for 30 seconds until it reduces to a light glaze coating the vegetables, then drizzle in the sesame oil.
Serve immediately while the bok choy is still crisp-tender.
tips: Cook the bok choy stems and leaves together but keep the total time short — overcooked bok choy turns watery and loses its bite.
Fresh shiitakes give more texture than dried here since the vegetable itself is the point, not a rehydrated mushroom flavor base.
nutritionNote: A genuinely low-oil, high-fiber vegetable side; the oyster sauce is the only sodium source, so this pairs well alongside a saltier main like char siu or soy sauce chicken without pushing the whole meal over on salt.

title: Century Egg and Chicken Congee
localTitle: Pi Dan Ji Rou Zhou (皮蛋鸡肉粥)
description: Rice simmered down into a smooth, savory porridge with shredded chicken, ginger and jelly-textured century egg — the dish Cantonese families reach for at breakfast, when sick, or any time something gentle is needed.

ingredients.note: plus more to loosen as it simmers

ingredients.item: ginger, half sliced and half julienned
century eggs, peeled and cut into small wedges
fried shallots or youtiao (Chinese fried dough), for serving

steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs mostly clear, then soak it in the 500ml water for 15 minutes — soaking shortens the simmer time and helps the grains break down evenly.
Bring the stock to a boil in a large pot, add the soaked rice with its soaking water and the sliced ginger, and return to a boil.
Reduce to a gentle simmer, partially cover, and cook for 25 minutes, stirring occasionally so the rice doesn't catch on the bottom.
Add the whole chicken thigh, submerging it in the porridge, and simmer 12-15 minutes until just cooked through.
Lift out the chicken, let it cool slightly, then shred it with two forks; set aside.
Continue simmering the congee 5-10 more minutes, stirring often, until the grains break down into a smooth, thick porridge — add hot water a splash at a time if it gets too thick.
Stir the shredded chicken and century egg wedges back into the pot, season with salt, white pepper and sesame oil, and warm through 1-2 minutes.
Ladle into bowls and top with julienned ginger and sliced scallion.
tips: Stirring occasionally as it simmers is what breaks the rice grains down into a creamy porridge instead of just soft rice in broth.
Century eggs taste strongest raw and cold — folding them in for the last couple of minutes rather than boiling them the whole time keeps their flavor milder for first-timers.
nutritionNote: A gentle, easy-to-digest one-bowl meal that's naturally low in fat; use low-sodium stock since congee is often eaten in larger portions than rice, and pair with a simple stir-fried green vegetable for fiber.

title: Beef Chow Fun
localTitle: Gan Chao Niu He (干炒牛河)
description: Wide rice noodles seared in a screaming-hot wok with velveted beef, bean sprouts and scallion until the noodles pick up a smoky char — the dish Cantonese cooks judge each other's wok skills by.

ingredients.item: flank steak, thinly sliced against the grain
fresh wide rice noodles (ho fun), separated

steps: Massage the baking soda into the beef, then mix in the soy sauce, cornstarch and water; marinate 15 minutes for a tender, velveted bite.
Whisk the dark soy sauce, light soy sauce, sugar and Shaoxing wine together in a small bowl.
Gently separate the rice noodles by hand, taking care not to tear them, since fresh ho fun is delicate and clumps together straight from the pack.
Heat a wok over the highest possible heat until it's smoking hot, add half the oil, and sear the beef in a single layer for 30-45 seconds per side until just browned; remove and set aside.

Add another tablespoon of oil and stir-fry the garlic and scallion whites 20 seconds, then add the noodles and 1 tablespoon of the sauce mixture. Use a folding motion rather than aggressive stirring to coat the noodles without breaking them, and let them sit undisturbed for 30 seconds at a time against the hot wok to pick up char.
Push the noodles aside, add the remaining oil, and pour in the rest of the sauce; toss briefly to coat.
Return the beef to the wok along with the bean sprouts and scallion greens. Toss everything together over the highest heat for 30-45 seconds until well combined.
Serve immediately while the noodles are still hot and smoky.
tips: Maximum heat the entire time is non-negotiable — a wok that isn't smoking hot steams the noodles instead of giving them the charred "wok hei" flavor the dish is named for.
Fold, don't stir, once the noodles are in the wok; vigorous stirring with a spatula is the most common way home cooks shred fresh ho fun into mush.
nutritionNote: A high-carb, high-sodium plate from the noodles and double soy sauce, so treat it as an occasional noodle night rather than a weekly staple, and serve a plain blanched vegetable alongside since the dish itself is light on fiber.

title: Hot and Sour Soup
description: A peppery, vinegar-forward broth thickened with cornstarch and loaded with tofu, wood ear mushroom and silky egg ribbons — the sharp, warming soup that opens a Sichuan-style home banquet.

ingredients.item: firm tofu, cut into thin strips
dried wood ear mushrooms, soaked in hot water 20 minutes and sliced
bamboo shoots, sliced into thin strips
lean pork, thinly sliced or shredded

ingredients.note: start with less, add more to taste

steps: Toss the sliced pork with the light soy sauce and cornstarch and let it sit 10 minutes while you prep everything else.
Bring the chicken stock to a simmer in a pot. Add the pork, stirring to separate the pieces, and cook 1-2 minutes until it turns opaque.
Add the tofu, wood ear mushrooms and bamboo shoots; simmer 3-4 minutes to let the flavors meld.
Stir in the vinegar, soy sauce, white pepper and salt; taste and adjust, keeping in mind the pepper's heat builds as it sits.
Give the cornstarch slurry a stir, since it settles fast, then drizzle it into the simmering soup while stirring constantly until it thickens enough to coat a spoon.
Stir the soup in one direction to create a gentle whirlpool, then slowly drizzle in the beaten eggs in a thin stream; let them set 10-15 seconds before stirring gently once more.
Ladle into bowls, drizzle with sesame oil, and top with sliced scallion.
Serve immediately, while the sourness and pepper are both at their sharpest.
tips: Add the white pepper gradually and taste as you go — it's the ingredient that makes this soup distinct from a plain sour soup, but it's easy to overdo.
Re-stir the cornstarch slurry right before pouring it in; it separates in under a minute sitting in the bowl.
nutritionNote: Vinegar-forward and naturally low in fat aside from a light drizzle of sesame oil at the end; the soy sauce and stock both add sodium, so use a low-sodium stock and serve smaller bowls as a soup course rather than the main protein.

title: Chinese Steamed Egg Custard
description: Beaten eggs loosened with warm stock and steamed low until barely set into a wobbly, custard-smooth savory pudding — the fastest, gentlest dish in the whole repertoire and the one kids ask for by name.

ingredients.note: about 1.5x the volume of the eggs

steps: Beat the eggs in a bowl until just combined, avoiding whipping in too much air, which causes bubbles in the finished custard.
Whisk in the warm stock or water and salt until fully blended.
Strain the mixture through a fine sieve into a shallow heatproof bowl to remove any bubbles or unmixed bits — this step is what gives the custard its glass-smooth surface.
Cover the bowl tightly with foil or a plate to keep condensation from dripping in and pitting the surface.

Set up a steamer with water at a gentle simmer, not a rolling boil, and steam the covered bowl over medium-low heat for 12-15 minutes, until the custard is just set with a slight wobble in the center.
Carefully remove the bowl and let it rest, covered, for 2 minutes.
Uncover, drizzle with sesame oil and a little light soy sauce, and scatter with scallion.
Serve warm, straight from the steaming bowl, with rice.
tips: Keep the steam gentle, not rolling — high heat is what causes the pitted, honeycombed texture instead of a smooth custard.
Straining the egg mixture takes ten extra seconds and is the single biggest difference between a silky restaurant version and a lumpy home one.
nutritionNote: Low in fat and easy to digest, with protein from the eggs and almost no added oil; pair with a vegetable stir-fry and rice for a complete meal, and use low-sodium stock if serving to young kids.
